solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 20dn.) Barely disguised lust and joy when penis centrally inserted

indicators.note: something disguised is given a different look, so the letters are rearranged out of recognition

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: centrally asks for the single letter standing in the exact middle of the following word

parts.note: the middle letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A smutty Private Eye picture of lust and joy only thinly veiled at a moment of intimacy.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of penis is added to the letters of lust and joy, and the eight are rearranged into ONLY JUST.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done barely is achieved by the narrowest margin, which is exactly what the phrase means.

clue.text: "Did a Business Secretary", i.e. communicated in an old-fashioned way?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, a joke: acted like Vince Cable, Business Secretary in the 2010 Coalition

explanation.surface: A satirical aside asking what it means to behave like the Business Secretary, suggesting he is out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: Vince Cable was the Liberal Democrat Business Secretary when this ran, so doing a Cable is jokily turned into a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cable was to send a telegram by wire, a method of messaging now long obsolete.

clue.text: Being smashed, discern void

indicators.note: something smashed is broken into bits that can be put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone too drunk to see straight finds their judgement emptied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashed' reads as drunk, and 'void' looks like an adjective, but it is the verb meaning cancel.
explanation.definitionFit: To void a contract or law is to annul it, which is the same as revoking or cancelling it.

clue.text: Limited by poor character, Tory leader — he should get rid of the pests

definitions.text: he should get rid of the pests

indicators.note: being limited by something means being hemmed in on both sides by it
something poor is in bad shape, so the word is put into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front

parts.note: the first letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A Tory leader hemmed in by a bad lot, with a hint that he should clear out the vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limited by poor character' reads as a jibe at a Tory leader's morals; the initial actually lands inside the scrambled word, not at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat catcher is employed to exterminate vermin, the pests the definition describes.

clue.text: Blair casually into "green"? That time's long gone

indicators.note: one thing put into another sits inside it, so these letters go within the next word

parts.note: sage is a grey-green colour
Tony Blair's first name in the matey shortened form 'Tone'

explanation.surface: A dig that Tony Blair dabbling in green politics belongs to an era that is long past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tone' is the chummy nickname for Tony; it is set inside the colour SAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone Age is the prehistoric period of stone tools, an epoch long vanished.

clue.text: A rich source for readers? Not Darling & co. now

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the government finance department, no longer run by Alistair Darling after the 2010 election

explanation.surface: A wry contrast between a bounty of books and the finance ministry that lost its Labour chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: Alistair Darling was Labour's Chancellor of the Exchequer until 2010, heading HM Treasury.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasury is a collection of literary gems, and also the name of the UK ministry of finance.

clue.text: Getting hard drug

parts.note: surface reading: acquiring a class A narcotic
setter's reading: a drug for getting an erection

explanation.surface: Someone obtaining a hard drug such as heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard drug' is a fixed phrase for addictive narcotics, but here 'getting hard' belongs together and describes what the pill does.
explanation.definitionFit: The well-known erectile dysfunction medicine works by helping men achieve an erection.

clue.text: City surrounded by capital provided by a jerk in vehicle

indicators.note: placed in something means put within it, so these letters go inside the next word

parts.note: a van is a vehicle
a tic is an involuntary twitch or jerk
taken as written

explanation.surface: Describes a city ringed by a capital, reached by someone twitching in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Vatican City is an independent city-state wholly enclosed by Rome, the Italian capital.

clue.text: City-backed politician, an arse

indicators.note: backed means turned to run the other way, so in a down entry it goes bottom to top

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, a crossword regular
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician bankrolled by the City of London is dismissed as an arse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City-backed' looks like financial backing from the Square Mile, but it means the city name read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The rump is the hindquarters or buttocks, so it is a polite synonym for the backside.

clue.text: Other side of Hyde Park's exit, covered in jelly, getting screwed

indicators.note: covered in means wrapped around by the next word
screwed up or twisted, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an exit is the way out at the end, pointing to the last letter of the word

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lurid scene of someone leaving Hyde Park smeared in jelly and having sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hyde' suggests the London park, but the definition means Mr Hyde, Stevenson's monster, whose better half is Dr Jekyll.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's novella, Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde are two sides of one split personality.

clue.text: A toothy thing after pussy remains underground here

indicators.note: after says the earlier-named piece comes second, so the order is swapped

parts.note: pussy is a pet name for a cat
taken as written
a comb has teeth

explanation.surface: A cat comes after something with teeth and then stays below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remains' looks like a verb meaning stays, but it is the noun: bodily remains are kept underground here.
explanation.definitionFit: A catacomb is an underground burial chamber, a place where the dead are interred.

clue.text: Shaky party leaders stopping hacks revealing what drives the Coalition's policies?

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so take the opening letter of each of the two words

parts.note: the initial letters of both words
stopping is ending
hacks as verb: chops or cuts

explanation.surface: Wobbly party bosses halting the phone-hacking journalists, which shows what really motivates the government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hacks' summons the 2011 phone-hacking scandal and journalists, but it is a verb meaning cuts. The Coalition is the 2010 Conservative-Liberal Democrat government.
explanation.definitionFit: Austerity reductions in public expenditure were the central theme of the 2010 Coalition's programme.

clue.text: Visually challenging magazine, 'Shagging US-style'

parts.note: Private Eye, the magazine in which this puzzle appears
balling is American slang for having sex

explanation.surface: A cover line for a magazine on American sex, hard on the eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine is the Eye itself, Private Eye; shagging is British slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeballing someone means staring them down, a confrontation carried out with the eyes.

clue.text: Nick, Nick is … dope

parts.note: both are slang for prison
to nick is to arrest or nab
taken as written

explanation.surface: A stammered police report or confession that Nick is a fool, or on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word has two different slang senses: the nick is jail, and to nick is to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is a slang name for marijuana, the drug produced from the hemp plant.

clue.text: Snapped Peter, grabbing poor PM, "Get in before the opposition does!"

definitions.text: Get in before the opposition does!

indicators.note: grabbing means seizing and holding inside one's grip
something snapped is broken, so the name is put back in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: poor here means in bad order, so the two letters swap places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Peter, perhaps Mandelson, snapping at an unpopular Prime Minister to strike first against the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: To pre-empt is to act first to forestall a rival, taking the initiative before they move.

clue.text: Hit peer badly, I beg you!

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters come out in a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A plea to someone to assault a member of the House of Lords clumsily.
explanation.definitionFit: Prithee is an archaic contraction of 'I pray thee', a polite way of pleading.

clue.text: One sort of HRT gets one cross — it's very infectious

parts.note: the indefinite article, meaning one

indicators.note: a sort of thing is a variant version, so the letters come in a different form

parts.note: taken as written
the indefinite article again, meaning one
a cross looks like the letter X

explanation.surface: A type of hormone replacement therapy that leaves one angry and passes on easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like angry but is the letter X. HRT is hormone replacement therapy.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthrax is a serious bacterial disease that can be caught from spores, so it is a dangerous infection.

clue.text: Brenda's staff showing pitiful respect

indicators.note: pitiful suggests a wretched state, so the letters are messed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Queen's household servants are not treating her with much deference.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so 'staff' is her rod of office, not her employees.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental rod a monarch carries as an emblem of royal authority.

clue.text: Camp follower was orgasmic on meeting "right-on" new leader

parts.note: Camp David, the US presidential retreat: David follows Camp
climaxed
R is the standard abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A camp hanger-on overcome with ecstasy on meeting a fashionable new party boss.
explanation.walkthrough: A camp follower is a hanger-on, but here it is the word that follows Camp in the name of the presidential retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: David Cameron became Prime Minister in 2010, so at the time he was the country's fresh head of government.

clue.text: Political commentator traps gutless supporter of Cameron, one getting stoned?

indicators.note: something trapped is held inside, so these letters go within the name

parts.note: Andrew Marr, the BBC political journalist

indicators.note: gutless means with the insides removed, leaving only the first and last letters

parts.note: a supporter of Cameron is a Tory; only its outer letters are kept

explanation.surface: A pundit corners a spineless Tory, who then ends up high on drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stoned' suggests intoxicated, but it means pelted with stones, as St Stephen was.
explanation.definitionFit: A martyr dies for their faith, and early Christian martyrs such as Stephen were killed by stoning.

clue.text: see 1dn.
Plenty of cracks from this bollocks parliamentarian

parts.note: bull is slang for nonsense, as is bollocks
a whip is the MP who enforces party discipline

explanation.surface: A parliamentarian talking rubbish produces plenty of wisecracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracks' suggests jokes, but it is the crack of a lash. Bollocks is British slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A bullwhip is a long, heavy lash whose tip breaks the sound barrier with a loud crack.

clue.text: Series of steps bar used to cover up stink

indicators.note: covering something up means enclosing it on both sides
something used is worn and knocked out of shape, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
hum is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: A pub was employed to hush up a scandal after a sequence of manoeuvres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Series of steps' sounds like a staircase or a plan, but it is a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhumba is a Cuban ballroom dance, a set routine of footwork.

clue.text: Starts to undo Gordon's lousy years, that's plain

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, one from each of those that follow

parts.note: the initial letter of each word

explanation.surface: A call to reverse Gordon Brown's wretched years in office, put bluntly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like it means obvious, but here it means unattractive. Gordon Brown was Labour Prime Minister 2007-10.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain face is unattractive, so plain serves as a polite synonym for unattractive in looks.

clue.text: Immediately repent welcoming Clegg's debut!

indicators.note: welcoming someone means taking them in, so a letter goes inside the word

parts.note: to atone is to make amends

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so take the opening letter of the name

parts.note: the first letter of the surname

explanation.surface: An urgent demand that Nick Clegg says sorry right now for his first outing.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg was the Liberal Democrat leader and Deputy PM who later apologised for breaking his tuition-fees pledge.
explanation.definitionFit: At once means without delay, a common adverbial phrase for straight away.

clue.text: Hattersley has a tip for one with cavalier attitude?

parts.note: Roy Hattersley, former Labour deputy leader
taken as written
to list is to tip or lean over, like a ship

explanation.surface: Roy Hattersley offers a hint to someone with a careless approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavalier' suggests offhand, but the Cavaliers were the King's supporters in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Cavaliers fought for Charles I, so someone of their outlook backs the monarchy.
